signOffConditionVerdicts.note: A backend is named for each of the five target platforms and no exception is recorded: DPAPI on Windows, libsecret on Linux, Keychain on macOS and iOS, Keystore on Android. A recorded backend with honest runtime reporting was preferred to a recorded exception, because an exception withholds the capability even where the platform can provide it, while an unavailable protector is already reported as not tamper-evident rather than assumed to work.

The write-failure behaviour is defined: the lost-record count increments and the station surfaces a non-zero count as a degraded state, so a lost audit record is counted rather than silently dropped. Whether the operation proceeds stays with DG-ROL, which settles it per command class.

guardPermissions.reason: The chain construction and the anchor are both settled, so the sink may report tamper-evidence once they are implemented. It stays false while the protector is unavailable at runtime, which is a state and not a gap: the chain alone is evident against editing and not against replacement.

A hash chain and an anchor are worth nothing over a write that may not have reached the disk, so settling them is what lets durability be claimed. The guard may become true once the durable write path the persistence design records is implemented.

The write-failure accounting behaviour is settled, so the counter may be incremented and surfaced. The register records its value as an expression, the sum of the dropped and failed audit-write counts, which this record does not change.

entries.value: A per-record hash chain. Each audit record stores a SHA-256 digest over its own canonical fields together with the digest of the record before it, so editing any field or removing any row breaks the chain at that point and every verification after it fails. Tampering is localised and provable rather than merely suspected. The construction needs no key, so it is identical on all five target platforms and cannot silently degrade on one of them. It detects tampering inside the file and says nothing about substitution of the whole file, which is the anchor concern settled separately. The existing posture is reinforced rather than replaced: AuditRecords already uses ON DELETE RESTRICT where every other table uses CASCADE, so pruning a session cannot remove audit records as a side effect, and the chain now makes a direct deletion detectable as well as refused.

settled.element: the protected chain anchor of D-DAT-05

entries.value: Yes. The chain head is written to the platform key store after each record, so a substituted database presents a head that does not match the stored anchor and the station reports it at startup rather than trusting the file it was handed. Per record rather than periodically, because a periodic anchor leaves every record written after the last one unprotected against replacement, which would make the protected window a number needing its own justification. The cost is accepted and recorded: one key-store write per audit record is the slowest step in the audit path. Where the platform protector is unavailable at runtime there is no anchor, and the station reports isTamperEvident() as false rather than claiming protection it does not have. The chain still stands in that state, so the log remains evident against editing and not against wholesale replacement.

settled.element: the AeroraPlatformKeyProtector backend for each target platform

entries.value: The sink increments AeroraCommandAuthorizer::lostAuditRecordCount(), which the register records as the sum of the dropped and failed audit-write counts, and a non-zero count is surfaced as a degraded state on SCR-SEC-03 and on the security posture page. A lost record is counted rather than silently dropped, which is Requirement 12 criterion 6. Whether the operation itself proceeds is deliberately not decided here: DG-ROL already settles it, denying an unauditable allow for the actuating classes payload and manual-control and counting but allowing it for command, parameter and mission. Restating it would create two rules that can disagree. Both alternatives were rejected in that record for reasons that still hold - denying everywhere turns a storage fault into a flight-control fault, so a full disk would begin refusing commands in flight including the command to land, and allowing everywhere leaves the trail with a hole exactly where actuation happened.
